# kind is rule, judgement or description, per docs/reference/agent_workflow.md ### Norm kinds. UNCLASSIFIED fails --check.
# observer is none, gate:<script>, lint:<file>, review:<skill> or prompt:<name>.

column5: description: "Owns the documentation rules: rule authority, folder placement, the document header and format rules, the concept-document and ADR obligations, and the lint gate over `docs/`."
scope: ["docs/", "devlog/"]
reader: [agent]

Skill files and prompt templates are not documentation. They reference or inline rules from policy documents. See [`agent_workflow.md`](../reference/agent_workflow.md#how-the-workflow-is-expressed) for those rules.

The document taxonomy -- what document types exist, their durability, and which policy or ADR governs each -- is the concept document [`documentation_taxonomy.md`](../reference/documentation_taxonomy.md). Diagnostic checklists for compliance live in the `doc-maintenance` skill, at `workflow/coding-agent/skills/doc-maintenance/SKILL.md`.
The kinds of norm, and the home each one has, are defined once in [`agent_workflow.md`](../reference/agent_workflow.md#norm-kinds). This section applies them to this file.

The ledger `scripts/lint/norm-ownership.tsv` records the kind and the observer of every prose line in this file and in `docs/development/prompt-authoring-conventions.md`. `scripts/check_norm_ownership.sh` holds the ledger against both files in both directions, so a new norm line arrives unclassified and an edited sentence loses its kind.
Where a norm has its home, and what makes a second copy a defect, is `principle-one-home-per-rule` at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/principle-one-home-per-rule/SKILL.md`.

Each `docs/` document belongs to **exactly one** folder: `reference/`, `policies/`, `development/`, or `adr/`. What each folder holds and why are in [`documentation_taxonomy.md`](../reference/documentation_taxonomy.md#folder-taxonomy). Superseded or awaiting-review ADRs live in `adr/archive/`.

Records outside `docs/` live in `devlog/`: the roadmap, the changelog, handovers, and discussion documents. Their placement and governance are in [`documentation_taxonomy.md`](../reference/documentation_taxonomy.md).

Architecture documents must not describe things a frozen layer does not yet do. The layer model, the per-layer freeze status, and the freeze rule live in [`system_overview.md`](../reference/system_overview.md#architecture-layer-model); `documentation_policy.md` applies them to document drafting.
Put a rule where the reader meets it. A rule governing Step 6 of the iteration belongs in the Step 6 entry of the workflow table, not in a separate document.

Workflow table Action cells hold one imperative sentence plus a link to the governing section; detail defers to the child document. Negative cases that mark a rule's limit stay in the table cell; illustrative examples belong in the child document.

New and changed prose meets ASD-STE100, with one exception. Where the work belongs to a well-specified technical domain and the reader works in that domain, its terms are the precise words, so use them and use no other field's. A word that names a thing in the domain is its term, and no list of banned words overrides it. A term the reader may not hold is defined at first use, per `principle-define-terminology-before-use` at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/principle-define-terminology-before-use/SKILL.md`.
Phrasing rules (a working subset of the full dictionary, not a replacement for it):

- Sentence structure. Active voice with a named actor, and a main clause that does not depend on its afterthought. The judgement is the `communication-principle-attach-as-you-read` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/communication-principle-attach-as-you-read/SKILL.md`.
- Short sentences. Aim under 20 words; one idea per sentence.
- One term, one meaning. Pick one word for a thing and keep it. Rotating synonyms ("volume" / "sandbox" / "workspace" for one object) is a defect.
- Common verbs. Prefer: is, has, uses, copies, reads, writes, runs, starts, stops, shows, checks, rejects. Avoid ornate verbs ("leverages", "facilitates", "encompasses").
- No idioms, no metaphors, no hedging ("somewhat", "fairly", "arguably").

- Define terminology before use. A term that can carry two meanings here, or one the repository does not define, is defined before the work relies on it ("Negative cases are scope constraints", then "Keep scope constraints in the cell"). The judgement is the `principle-define-terminology-before-use` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/principle-define-terminology-before-use/SKILL.md`.
- STE100 simplifies structure and verbs, not precision.
- State the allowed form and name the action. Judgement: `communication-principle-write-for-the-reader`.
Evaluate prose with two tests:
- **Delete test.** The judgement is the `communication-principle-cut-what-carries-nothing` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/communication-principle-cut-what-carries-nothing/SKILL.md`.

- **Literal-reader test.** A literal reader follows the words exactly and infers no intent. Could the reader turn the sentence into a task, an action, or an inference that was not intended? If yes, rephrase it with the phrasing rules.

**Reserved technical terms** are defined in [`docs/reference/terminology.md`](../reference/terminology.md). When a policy, concept, or architecture document uses a reserved term in its technical sense, link to the term's section on first mention. Do not redefine a reserved term locally.
All documents in `docs/` open with a consistent header block, so status and scope are visible without reading the body and `grep -n "^##"` returns a usable section map.
**Standard opening sequence:**
Rules:
- `**Status:**` is the first line after the title on all discussion documents (story, study, design, report). No preamble before it.
- Superseded and resolved documents carry a blockquote redirect immediately after the status line, naming the target document.
- Reference and policy documents carry no status line -- the layer-freeze table in `system_overview.md` governs them.
- ADR headers and entry structure are defined in [`adr_policy.md`](adr_policy.md), not here.
- Top-level sections use `##`; subsections use `###`. Use `####` only inside long task lists where grouping is genuinely needed -- not for general document structure.

- Policy files (`docs/**/*_policy.md`) open with YAML frontmatter holding a `description` and a `scope`, then a blank line, then the `# <Title>` heading. `reader` names who must read the document to do their job: one or more of `agent`, `operator` and `maintainer`. A document serving only the maintainer does not ship, so the frontmatter gate fails one that sits in a shipping folder, which is `docs/reference/` or `docs/policies/`.
- `description` is one quoted line naming the rules the file owns. `scope` is a single-line flow list of the records and runbooks the file governs.
Documents use plain ASCII punctuation.
- Write a dash as a space-separated hyphen (` - `), or as a double hyphen (`--`) in prose. In headings, use the space-separated form.
- To reference a document or section, write its name, or link with an anchor.
- Write status markers as `[x]` / `[ ]` (tables) or `- [x]` / `- [ ]` (lists). Do not use checkmark or cross emoji.
- Do not use non-ASCII punctuation (section sign U+00A7, pilcrow U+00B6) or control and formatting symbols (space glyphs, chapter symbols).

**Exception -- ASCII-art diagrams.** Box-drawing characters (U+2502 vertical, U+251C left tee, U+2514 corner, U+2500 horizontal) may appear inside ASCII-art diagrams (for example directory trees), where they carry the diagram's geometry. Use them nowhere else; convert banners, table rules, and decoration to ASCII hyphens.

Prose is one paragraph per physical line, however long the line. Never break inside a paragraph -- not at sentence boundaries, not at a column limit; editors and viewers soft-wrap. Hard breaks separate blocks only: paragraphs, headings, list items. The rule covers all prose: guidance blocks, `AGENTS.md`, provider-layer files. Code comments wrap at about 80 columns. Fenced code blocks and table rows are exempt.

Make references with links. Link what the reader might need next; a well-linked document is a good one. Link a document the reader may need to open; otherwise write its name. Inline code (backticks) is not a substitute for a link.

A link resolves where its document is read. A document under `reference/` or `policies/` ships into the container, where the repository tree is absent, so a link from it reaches only a path that ships: link a shipped document by its image path, or by the relative form the two bundled folders keep. A document that ships nowhere -- a record, an ADR, a development document -- is named in a code span carrying its repository path, never linked. The `record-links` lint rule fails the gate on a link that resolves only in the repository.

Prefer durable targets. Link a durable document to the durable document that records the fact, not to its evidence: documentation and policy link to an ADR, and the ADR links to the handover that evidences its decision. Where the citing document ships and the durable target does not, name the target instead of linking it. When a durable document must name transient evidence, write the name as plain text and do not link it.

Place handoff links at the point of use. When a workflow document (such as `iteration_policy.md`) hands off to a subprocess governed by a child policy document, link that policy where the handoff happens -- not only in a References table -- and name the specific section. A References table is navigation, not a handoff.

Form the link precisely. Step-level references carry a section anchor; document-level references use a plain document link. When an agent may need to locate a section programmatically, give a grep command instead of a link.

The numbering scheme is stated once, in the project convention `.agents/skills/numbering/SKILL.md`: which unit takes a number, which takes an identity code, the form of a reference, the chat label, and how a chat pick reaches a record. This section states the one rule the convention does not carry.
When many references point to one item, move it to a heading.

Structure documents so agents can grep section headers and range-read only what they need. Every section an agent might need in isolation has a `##` or `###` header -- unnamed blocks are not grep-targetable.
A document that must be read in full to extract one fact is structured wrong. If a fact is needed at a specific moment in a workflow, put it in a named section or inline it at the point of use.

When a policy or convention states a document's section order, present it as a fenced Markdown skeleton, with each section's purpose on the line below its heading in angle brackets, so the block doubles as a fill-in template:

Use this shape for every document type, in every policy. Prefer it to a table of sections and purposes: order and purpose are read together, and the block is copied directly into a new document. Use a table only when a type carries a column the skeleton cannot, such as the valid state transitions of a status table.

Pick the folder category before drafting. Update only the sections the change affects -- targeted edits beat rewrites. Add a document only when it serves a structural purpose no existing document covers.

Before writing an ADR or a reference document, propose the skeleton in chat -- section list and what each section holds -- and get operator confirmation. Write prose only against the confirmed skeleton. Drafting full prose before the structure is agreed has produced full rewrites. The skeleton costs minutes; a rewrite costs more.

The judgement for a durable record is the `communication-principle-write-for-the-reader` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/communication-principle-write-for-the-reader/SKILL.md`. That skill is the judgement's only home; the concept document [`documentation_taxonomy.md`](../reference/documentation_taxonomy.md) classifies what endures.

A design record carries no question-and-reply pair, and every question it lists is still open. Keep a short section of the designs that were considered and rejected, with the reason for each, and put the final design at the forefront of the document.
A reference document describes its layer as built. A sentence that uses one of these words usually marks a forecast: `will` `plan` `future` `later` `eventually` `may support`. A TODO item is one too.
The judgement is the `communication-principle-dont-forecast-undone-work` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/communication-principle-dont-forecast-undone-work/SKILL.md`.

Reference documents keep their code examples current. Every code block, variable name, path, and function signature matches the implementation as built. A document updated across several sessions collects stale examples that contradict the system as built; when you update such a document, check each example against the implementation and update the ones that changed.
This section holds the document lint rules and the gate that enforces them. It does not cover code lint; code gates are not documentation policy.

The repository holds zero Markdown lint findings. The gate runs `markdownlint-cli2` with the repository config `.markdownlint-cli2.mjs`. A finding is a defect: fix it in the same change. Run the gate with `make lint` or `bash scripts/lint.sh`.

The config enables the rules that match this policy. It disables `MD013` because [`### Line wrapping`](#line-wrapping) forbids breaking prose at a column limit, and `MD060` because the repository writes compact tables. Three repository rules enforce parts of this policy: `doc-ascii` (plain-ASCII prose, in `scripts/lint/doc-ascii.mjs`, per [`### Character set`](#character-set)), `doc-wrap` (one paragraph per physical line, in `scripts/lint/doc-wrap.mjs`, per [`### Line wrapping`](#line-wrapping)), and `record-links` (link targets exist and fragments name a heading, in `scripts/lint/record-links.mjs`). Do not silence a finding with a per-file disable; fix the text or change the config.

A rule the config registers but does not enable is a defect. `config.default` is `false`, so a rule named nowhere in the config never runs and reports nothing, and the gate prints a clean verdict over an empty rule set. `record-links` sat in that state: this list named two rules, the config registered three and enabled two, and the link gate reported nothing for the life of the config. Naming a rule here and enabling it there are one obligation.
This section holds the obligations that apply per document type; it describes no genre.

A concept document is standalone and content-complete: a reader new to the area understands the model and what it guarantees without another document. Outbound links are for further reading, not prerequisites.
A concept document links to its ADR and does not restate the ADR's record.

Restate requirements as user-observable guarantees, without seam vocabulary -- requirement numbers, promotion history, internal component names. The ADR owns the numbering, the design mapping, and the history; the concept doc owns the readable form.

Describe components as interfaces, contracts, or diagrams. Exact commands and variable values appear only for external interactions the harness does not control (for example `docker` CLI mappings). Internal command sequences, function names, and file paths belong in the architecture docs or the ADR.
When and how to create or distill an ADR: see [`adr_policy.md`](adr_policy.md) -- When an ADR begins.

**Principle.** A closed record's content does not change; whether a record is durable or transient is classified in the concept document [`documentation_taxonomy.md`](../reference/documentation_taxonomy.md#durability). It gains the marker its type carries, and a record that tracks state also gains a successor entry. The mechanic follows what the record is for: a record that states what is true is corrected in place, and a record that tracks open and closed tasks is corrected by addition.

**Direction.** A closed record is corrected at the operator's direction. The agent may notice a correction and propose it in one line, and may not apply one unasked. The agent never deletes a record; deletion is an operator action. Applying a correction is bounded by two stops and one smell:
- **Stop -- the correction changes the unit's scope or carries new work.** New work belongs in a new iteration.
- **Stop -- an edit to a closed record would carry no marker.** An untraceable edit is a rewrite, not a correction.

- **Smell -- folding the correction needs an interactive rebase with several conflict edits.** Report the smell and stop; the operator rules on it. Past that size the instrument is a port, not a correction; the git policy names the operation in its reference table.

**Propagation.** A correction inherits the record set of the unit it corrects. A unit that changed code, a task description and a handover is corrected in all three, and every closed record among them takes its marker. A correction that leaves a closed record contradicting its successor is incomplete.
**Archival is not amendment.** Moving a closed milestone's entries from the roadmap to the changelog is a length boundary, not a correction, and carries no marker.
**Forms by document type:**
If a document the agent expects is absent:
- The referencing link carries a `[REMOVED]` marker: the absence is expected. No error.
- The referencing link has no `[REMOVED]` marker: flag an error and ask the operator. Do not assume the document is optional; do not proceed unresolved.

This document states the authoring rules for prompts and skills. It answers four questions: what structure a workflow document has, what belongs in a runbook versus an advisor, how to scope a prompt's subject, and how to identify a workflow document. It is the home for the workflow-document presentation rules that the `/document` stub defers here.
The per-prompt quality passes read this document before they edit a prompt. The `fanout` doc pass reads it before it edits that prompt. Any session that writes a new prompt or skill reads it first.

This document owns the authoring bar for workflow documents. The conceptual model behind them stays in [`agent_workflow.md`](../reference/agent_workflow.md) - the layers, the loading mechanism, and the authority hierarchy. That document says what a prompt or skill is; this document says how to write one. A rule that states a fact about the model, not a rule about writing, lives in `agent_workflow.md`.

The authoring rules borrow from two external references: Claude's Skill authoring best practices (`https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices`) and mattpocock's `writing-for-agents` skill (`https://github.com/mattpocock/skills`, under `skills/productivity/writing-for-agents`). Both describe levers for writing documents an agent consumes. The repository's own prompt and skill set is the primary source; the references explain the reasoning. Read this document for the rules.
A document an agent consumes is one of three types. The type determines where it lives and how it is written.
**Policy** documents hold the authoritative rules. Write a rule only into a policy document in `docs/policies/`, `docs/reference/`, `docs/reference/`, or `docs/development/`.
**Reference** documents state facts consulted on demand. They define terms, list options, or hold data. A reference document states no rule; it serves the rules that live in policy.

**Workflow** documents are prompts and skills. They are execution helpers and iteration tooling. They are consumers of the policy documents: they reference the rules there, or inline a distillation for context efficiency. A workflow document never carries an authoritative rule. It may carry a judgement, in a principle skill, and that skill is the judgement's only home. This document calls them workflow documents; [`documentation_policy.md`](../policies/documentation_policy.md) excludes them from its scope by the same boundary.
Two tests identify a workflow document:
1. **Who invokes it.** A prompt runs at the operator's word (`/iter`, `/plan`). A skill runs at the model's or the operator's invocation. A policy or reference document is read, not invoked.

2. **Does it carry authoritative rules?** If removing the document leaves a rule unstated anywhere, the document carries that rule and is policy, not workflow. A workflow document that is the only home of a rule is miswritten.

A third test separates the forms a workflow document takes. Is it steps, reference, or judgement? A runbook holds ordered steps. A reference holds facts. An advisor holds judgements and a diagnostic checklist. This distinction shapes the structure, described below.

The three-layer model for where prompts and skills live is in [`agent_workflow.md`](../reference/agent_workflow.md). The provider layer, the sandbox layer, and the user layer load different sets. An author writes for the layer the prompt or skill is baked into and does not change the loading mechanism.

A workflow document is built from ordered steps, reference, or both. The core decision is where each piece of content sits on the information hierarchy. The hierarchy ranges from most immediately needed to most deferred:
1. **In-file step** is the primary tier. It is what the agent does, in order. Every run needs it.
2. **In-file reference** is consulted on demand. It is a set of rules or facts the agent reaches for when a step needs it.

3. **Disclosed reference** is pushed into a separate file, reached by a context pointer, and loaded only when the pointer fires. It spans a sibling file in the same folder through fully external reference.

Progressive disclosure is the move down the ladder, out of the main file and behind a pointer. It keeps the top legible. It protects the hierarchy; it is not a token saving alone. A document that branches is the cleanest disclosure test: inline what every branch needs, and disclose what only some branches reach.

The failure mode is sprawl: a document too long even when every line is live. Attention thins across the excess. The cure is the ladder: disclose reference behind pointers and split by branch so each path carries only what it needs.

Co-location is the within-file companion. Keep a concept's definition, rules, and caveats under one heading rather than scattered. The test: the document should read like documentation written for the agent. Grouped material reads that way; scattered material does not.

**Match the precision to the stakes.** An instruction narrows as its stakes rise: how far a wrong move reaches, whether it can be undone, and whether anything reports it. The judgement is the `principle-match-precision-to-stakes` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/principle-match-precision-to-stakes/SKILL.md`.

**No magic constants in a snippet.** The judgement is the `communication-principle-name-the-value-not-a-literal` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/communication-principle-name-the-value-not-a-literal/SKILL.md`.

A **runbook** is a prompt or skill that holds ordered steps. Each step ends on a criterion that says when the step is done; the judgement is the `principle-say-what-done-looks-like` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/principle-say-what-done-looks-like/SKILL.md`. The reference region of a prompt is different: it lists rules consulted on demand and has no step to finish.

The loop prompts (`/iter`, `/plan`, `/sidequest`, `/milestone-start`, `/milestone-close`) are runbooks. Their steps map the iteration and milestone workflow procedures, and the rules stay in the policy documents.

An **advisor** is a prompt or skill that holds reference and judgement, run against a document or a code change to find defects. It is a diagnostic checklist: it identifies what has gone wrong, not what to do instead. The corresponding prescriptive rules live in the policy and the conventions. An audit prompt must not carry an authoritative rule, because a skill is a fast path, not a source of truth.

The advisor-role split is explicit: the advisor names its role, states when to run it, and constructs a brief. The triage and consensus steps after the advisor returns are part of the runbook that dispatched it.

A **skill** is an execution helper, distinct from a prompt by mechanism not by writing. It is a fast path to a rule that lives in policy. A rule that exists only in a skill is not authoritative. An inline distillation of a rule is a convenience copy; it may go stale, and that is acceptable only because it is not the source of truth. A judgement is the other case: nothing detects its breach, and it lives with the document that produces it, per [`agent_workflow.md`](../reference/agent_workflow.md#norm-kinds) `### Norm kinds`.

**Where a check goes is a judgement.** A check reads evidence and produces a decision, so its placement is stated in the `principle-check-placement` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/principle-check-placement/SKILL.md`, and a skill that holds checks points there.

Subagents receive `pi -p` with a brief; the same brief-writing rules apply. The `/task-queue` prompt forks a fresh subagent per task with a brief that names the task, its segments, its owned files, its report, and the worker protocol.
A prompt opens with frontmatter and a body. The frontmatter fields are the prompt's context pointers: they decide when the agent or the operator reaches the document.

**Description.** State what the prompt does and when to use it. Include the trigger terms a reader or the model would say or think. The description is the top-level pointer, forced to stay loaded. Front-load the triggering word, keep one trigger per branch, and cut anything the body already carries. Write the description in the imperative or the third person; pick one for the prompt. The repo prompt set is split: the loop prompts and `task-queue` use the imperative (`iter`: "Open a new iteration..."), `plan` uses the third person ("Runs a plan session... Routes the outcome"). Third person reads better where several sentences share one subject; do not claim one voice for all. The description names the prompt's subject: `iter` names every workflow type it accepts, `milestone-close` names the fractal close, `task-queue` names the operator decision at segment boundaries. The frontmatter is YAML, so a malformed value breaks the prompt. A plain (unquoted) value cannot hold a colon, a leading dash, or a trailing colon, because YAML reads each as structure rather than as text; a value holding any of the three must be wrapped in double quotes, with any double quote inside it escaped. An apostrophe in a plain value is legal and needs no quoting. Pi drops a prompt whose frontmatter does not parse without a message in the session, so the prompt never appears in the command list. `scripts/check_frontmatter.sh` parses every prompt, skill and policy frontmatter in the tree and fails the gate on a block that does not parse, so the rule is enforced by the gate rather than left to the author.
**Argument hint.** Where the prompt accepts an argument, state the argument's shape and whether it is optional. The `iter` prompt names its accepted type words; `plan` marks its argument required.

**Skill frontmatter.** A skill opens with `name` and `description`. `disable-model-invocation: true` removes a skill from the model's prompt, so the model can neither discover nor fire it; only the operator invokes it, by typing its name. Set it on a skill the operator fires deliberately: the two quality skills and the two loop runbooks set it in this tree. A judgement skill does not set it, because a writer reaches for a judgement mid-draft and must find it, and the field's value is a boolean, held by the frontmatter gate. A description on a hidden skill is read from the operator's skill list, so write it for the operator and not for the model. A model-invoked skill keeps a description the agent uses for discovery. A router skill names the others and when to reach for each, for when user-invoked skills multiply past what the operator can remember.

**Suggested skill name.** The scheme below is a suggestion, not a rule; nothing in the tree checks a skill name, and the norm-ownership ledger records it as a judgement with no observer. A name states the class and then the judgement, so a reader scanning the skill list can tell what a skill is without opening it. A principle follows `[<domain>-]principle-<judgement>`: a bare `principle-` when the judgement holds for any agentic work, and the domain prefix when it is confined to one, as in `principle-guard-the-context-window`, `communication-principle-write-for-the-reader`, and `bash-coding-principle-<judgement>` for language-specific work. The scheme shadows the one the `poteto` skill set uses at its fork source, `pstack`, so a name states the class and never the provenance; the skill's maintenance record states where it came from. Every other skill follows `<verb-noun>`, one short action word chosen for the general situation that invokes it, so that `/<action>` reads to the operator as "do <action>", the same shape as `node run <action>` and `uv run <action>`. A mode keeps the `-mode` suffix `poteto-mode` established.
**Body order.** A finished workflow document follows a stable order:

1. **The opening template line.** A main-agent prompt opens with `> $@` after the frontmatter, then a title and a `Scope` declaration that states the prompt's boundary. A runbook without this declaration makes a misplaced title indistinguishable from a missing one.

2. **Purpose** states what the prompt or skill is for and what it is not. The task-queue prompt leads with what it is a primitive for, then names what it is not in its "Not this template" routing, inside "When to use".

3. **When to use** states the conditions that invoke it and the routing: what it is for, and what replaces it in the cases it is not for. The task-queue prompt names `iter.md` and `fanout-run.md` as the not-this-template cases.

4. **The steps or the reference region** carries the work. A runbook orders its steps and ends each on a completion criterion; the judgement is the `principle-say-what-done-looks-like` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/principle-say-what-done-looks-like/SKILL.md`. A reference region lists rules consulted on demand, so it has no step to finish.

5. **The handoff.** A runbook that ends by handing to another prompt names the boundary. The judgement is the `communication-principle-hand-off-by-naming-the-boundary` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/communication-principle-hand-off-by-naming-the-boundary/SKILL.md`. A prompt that ends inside its own scope omits it.
6. **Non-goals** states what the prompt deliberately does not do, so the agent does not silently extend scope.

7. **Failure modes and invariants** close a runbook: what can go wrong and what the work must not break. The run-style and work-style prompts (`sequential-work`, `parallel-work`, `fanout-run`) and `task-queue` carry them.

**The project conventions block.** A workflow document that reads or writes project records opens with a `## Project conventions` section before its first step. It lists the conventions the document uses, each read at `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, and states the failure when that file is absent or holds the seeded stub: control passes to the agent, which decides with the steering it has loaded, and the workflow prescribes no fallback. The block names the convention, never the project's paths - the workflow keeps the procedure and the project's convention-skill holds the structure - so a project with a different layout is served by its own skill. The fourteen loop prompts and the six module skills are the model, and `gm` is the minimal case.

The workflow-document presentation rules that the `/document` stub defers here complete the structure: prose in the body follows the writing standards in `documentation_policy.md`. No step-by-step walkthrough repeats a rule the policy already states; the prompt links to the policy at the point of handoff. A prompt is never the only home of a rule.

**One subject per prompt.** The subject is what the prompt hands on: one artifact to one next step. A prompt that hands on two artifacts, or hands one to two next steps, is two prompts, or a runbook that dispatches two sub-cases. The judgement is `principle-own-the-scope-you-declare` at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/principle-own-the-scope-you-declare/SKILL.md`.

Scope earlier shapes the authoring. A prompt's scope statement must not contradict its own success criteria. Name the in-scope targets explicitly. If a criterion can only be met by a change that looks out of scope, make the criterion flag-only or name the target. This restates the prompt-scope discipline in [`iteration_policy.md`](../policies/iteration_policy.md), which applies it both at runtime and to the main agent authoring the prompt. Write the scope so the contradiction cannot arise.

A prompt that hands off to a sub-agent states the target's whole owned-file set, not a per-unit list, and remaps the sandbox boundary to the worktree. The brief-construction lesson applies at authoring time: a file set must be closed under the test surface, and the closure is computed by searching the test tree for each changed file's basename. The `/task-queue` prompt (`.agents/drafts/task-queue.md`, draft pending operator review) models this: it defines fork, join, and re-queue as the machinery, and the caller supplies the tasks and their owned files.

**Skill names and descriptions route a skill.** A skill is advertised by its name and its description, and its body loads only after a reader decides, so those two fields carry the words that route it, and the description summarises to the name. The judgement is the `principle-effective-skill-routing` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/principle-effective-skill-routing/SKILL.md`.
A workflow document is a consumer of the policy documents. It may inline a distillation of a rule for context efficiency, under two constraints:
1. The rule still exists in a policy document. The inline is a fast path to it, never a replacement.
2. The inline is labelled as a convenience copy where its staleness would mislead. An inlined rule that a reader takes as current must carry its pointer to the policy.

This is the canonical-owner test applied to prompts and skills. When a rule appears in a workflow document and in a policy document, an agent reads the policy for the authoritative form and the workflow document for the fast path. The policy is the canonical owner.

Construct defensively against two decay modes, both the delete test applied to an instruction surface: `communication-principle-cut-what-carries-nothing` at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/communication-principle-cut-what-carries-nothing/SKILL.md`. A **no-op** is an instruction the agent already obeys by default. **Stale accumulation** is content kept because removing it feels risky.

The diagnostic register for these checks is `## The diagnostic register` in the [`doc-maintenance`](../../workflow/coding-agent/skills/doc-maintenance/SKILL.md) skill. The prescriptive rules are here and in `documentation_policy.md` (its `### Rule placement`); the register lists the signs to look for. The canonical-owner test appears in both, by design: the two registers serve different readers.

A workflow document owns the scope it declares, holds everything that scope owes, and describes no work outside it. The judgement is the `principle-own-the-scope-you-declare` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/principle-own-the-scope-you-declare/SKILL.md`, which is its only home. A top-down view of the whole flow belongs to a concept document or an ADR, and that document names the steps rather than replacing them.

A runbook that ends by handing to another prompt names the boundary in four moves. The judgement is the `communication-principle-hand-off-by-naming-the-boundary` skill at `$AGENT_HOME/agent/skills/communication-principle-hand-off-by-naming-the-boundary/SKILL.md`, which is its only home. Four prompts apply the shape: [`/iter`](../../workflow/coding-agent/prompts/iter.md) and [`/plan`](../../workflow/coding-agent/prompts/plan.md) hand to `/wrapup` Part B, [`/sidequest`](../../workflow/coding-agent/prompts/sidequest.md) hands the same way, and [`/document`](../../workflow/coding-agent/prompts/document.md) hands at its close.

A prompt runs at its image path. The harness prompts run from `/opt/workflow/agent/prompts/`, from `src/reasoning/agent/prompts/`. A workflow module's prompts run from the module's own root, `/opt/workflow/agent/modules/<module>/prompts/`, from `workflow/<module>/prompts/`, because the module is the unit a provider enables or leaves out. A provider's own prompt runs from that provider's root: pi's `pi-agent.md` runs from `$AGENT_HOME/agent/prompts/` -- `/home/agentuser/.pi/agent/prompts/` -- which the image seeds from `src/reasoning/providers/pi/config/agent/prompts/` through the config template. The repository tree is not there. The link check resolves a link in an instruction file in the image's path space rather than the repository's, so a target that exists only in the repository is a finding, and a link in the old repository-relative form no longer passes.

A prompt links a document that ships. The policy corpus ships at `/opt/sandbox/docs/policies/`, and the reference layer ships beside it at `/opt/sandbox/docs/reference/`. The link names the path the document has in the image, which reads the same from every instruction root and needs no depth arithmetic. A prompt in one instruction root links a document in another by the image path, not the source path.

A prompt names a document that does not ship -- a record, a draft, an ADR, a development document -- in plain text or a code span. Name it by the path a reader can find, and do not link it: the link would pass no reader in the container and fail the check. A reference to a project file, such as the project `AGENTS.md` or `devlog/roadmap.md`, is the same case, because the project tree is the reader's working directory rather than the prompt's.

When the content behind the reference matters to the agent working in the container, it belongs in the prompt or in a shipped file, and the record is the place the decision is argued -- not the place the running agent is sent.

The same rule covers the inverse: a rule whose only home is a record is unreachable from the container, whether or not a link points at it. If the agent must obey it, it is stated where the agent reads.

The rule holds for a bundled document too. A document under `docs/reference/` or `docs/policies/` ships into the container, where the repository tree is absent, so a link from it reaches only a path that ships: a relative link between the two bundled folders resolves because their destinations keep the repository's shape, and an image path resolves for the same reason. A target that ships nowhere -- a record, an ADR, a development document -- is named in a code span carrying its repository path, never linked. [`record-links.mjs`](../../scripts/lint/record-links.mjs) fails the gate on a link from a shipped file that resolves only in the repository.

A workflow document's name states its subject, not its mechanism. Prefer a noun phrase that names the work (`task-queue`, `milestone-close`) or a gerund that names the activity (`documentation-pass`). Avoid vague names (`helper`, `utils`) and names that restate the loading mechanism.
A name changes when its scope changes. Rename a document whose name no longer matches its subject, and run a doc pass over it at the same time.

A prompt or skill that is not yet operator-reviewed is a draft. The durable gate is the location: drafts live in `.agents/drafts/` -- a root the frontmatter gate does not scan, the dispatch conventions do not read, and live dispatch never references -- so an unreviewed prompt is structurally unreachable by the run paths that would trust it. The file itself carries `**Status:** draft` as the human-readable marker. A draft is released from draft status only with explicit operator direction; the release is one commit that moves the file from `drafts/` into its live root (or the agent-facing prompt tree), runs a documentation pass over it at the same time, and the move is the promotion -- there is no separate promotion step to forget. A prompt written by an autonomous worker unit is a draft by default, whatever its author claimed; the `maintenance` dispatch prompt's premature switch-over (it became load-bearing in the session that wrote it, and carried a merge-back contract that produced seven `merge:` commits) is the recorded incident this gate exists to stop.

The per-prompt quality passes read this document and apply it to one prompt each, starting with `/task-queue`. Each pass must name what it changed and why against a specific rule here. The `fanout` doc pass applies the same reading to that prompt. A session that writes a new prompt or skill applies it at authoring time.
